# GMAW, FCAW and MCAW on Mild Steel Pipe

Pipe welding pays. Structural welders on plate top out around $45/hr in Alberta. Pipe welders on rig-up, refinery turnaround, or pipeline work? $65-90/hr, often with per-diem. The reason: pipe welds are harder to make sound, harder to inspect, and welders who can pass X-ray on pipe are rare. This lesson is your ticket into that pay grade.

---

## Pipe positions — memorize these visually

| Position | Pipe orientation | Weld path | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1G / 1GR** | Horizontal (axis horizontal), **rotated during welding** | Welder holds gun at ~12 o'clock, pipe rotates past | Easiest |
| **2G** | Vertical (axis vertical), pipe fixed | Weld runs horizontally around pipe (like a belt) | Medium |
| **5G** | Horizontal (axis horizontal), **pipe fixed** | Welder walks around pipe, welds in every position from 12 to 6 o'clock | Hard |
| **6G** | 45° angle (axis at 45°), pipe fixed | Every position at every angle — the hardest common pipe test | Hardest |

**1GR "rolled" is the sweet spot for practice** — you rotate the pipe on rollers or by hand while welding at 12 o'clock. Once you have solid technique rolled, progress to fixed positions.

---

## Standard industrial procedures for mild steel pipe

Two common combinations in Alberta pipe work:[^1][^2]

### Procedure A: Pipeline / downhill root
Used for cross-country pipeline, refinery process piping where speed matters and X-ray is the acceptance criterion.

- **Root pass:** GMAW short-arc, downhill (12 to 6), 0.035" ER70S-6, 75/25 Ar/CO2, 120-150 A / 17-19 V
- **Hot pass:** FCAW-G, uphill (6 to 12), 0.045" E71T-1, 75/25 Ar/CO2, 180-200 A / 22-24 V
- **Fill/cap:** FCAW-G, uphill, same wire, 200-240 A / 24-27 V

**Why downhill root:** the small, controlled short-arc puddle plus gravity assist gives fast, consistent penetration. Traditional stick (SMAW) pipeliners used cellulose (E6010) downhill for exactly the same reason.

### Procedure B: Refinery / uphill throughout
Used for high-pressure, code-critical piping (ASME B31.1, B31.3).

- **Root pass:** GMAW-P (pulsed), uphill, 0.035" ER70S-6, 90/10 Ar/CO2, machine-programmed pulse parameters (varies by machine)
- **Hot / fill / cap:** FCAW-G uphill, 0.045" E71T-1, standard parameters

**GMAW-P root uphill** is slower than downhill short-arc but gives cleaner sidewall fusion. Preferred for pressure vessel–grade pipe in refineries.

---

## The 5G walk — the signature pipe welder skill

5G pipe (fixed horizontal) requires you to weld in **every possible position** as you walk around the pipe:[^1]

**On the top half (12 to 3 o'clock):** you're welding overhead-ish → reduce amperage, small puddle, faster travel
**Around 3 o'clock (3 side):** vertical up position, standard technique
**On the bottom half (3 to 6):** progressing into flat-ish position at 6 o'clock

Traditional 5G downhill:
- Start at 12 o'clock, weld to 6 o'clock on one side
- Move to the other side of the pipe, start at 12, weld to 6
- Repeat with each pass

Uphill 5G:
- Start at 6 o'clock, weld up to 12 on one side
- Other side, 6 to 12
- Slower but stronger welds

**A well-executed 5G root pass on pipe with wire-feed processes shows a smooth, uniform bead all the way around with no starts/stops visible.**

---

## Downhill root technique (GMAW short-arc)

The signature move of pipeline welders:[^1][^5]

- **Wire:** 0.035" ER70S-6 or ER70S-3 (cheaper, adequate for most)
- **Gas:** 75/25 Ar/CO2 (smoother) or 100% CO2 (deeper penetration but more spatter)
- **Amperage/Voltage:** 120-150 A / 17-19 V (true short-arc, sounds like frying bacon)
- **Travel direction:** DOWNHILL (12 to 6)
- **Gun angle:** 5-15° drag (backhand) — even downhill, you drag the arc behind
- **Speed:** fast — the small puddle plus gravity assist means you can outrun most puddle problems
- **Keyhole:** small keyhole through the root; you're feeding the wire into the leading edge as you descend

**Critical:** if the wire tries to burn back to the contact tip, your voltage is too low OR your CTWD is too short. Adjust before you ruin the joint.

---

## Uphill fill/cap technique (FCAW-G)

After root, switch guns to 0.045" FCAW-G and go UPHILL:[^6]

- **Wire:** 0.045" E71T-1
- **Gas:** 75/25 Ar/CO2
- **Amperage/Voltage:** 200-240 A fill / 200-220 A cap
- **Travel direction:** UPHILL (6 to 12)
- **Gun angle:** 5-15° drag angle
- **Weave:** slight side-to-side triangular weave, pause at toes
- **Speed:** slow, watch the puddle — E71T-1 slag freezes fast which lets you run all-position

---

## Joint prep for wire-feed on pipe

Standard prep for GMAW/FCAW pipe root:[^3][^4]

- **Bevel:** 30° per side = 60° included angle (some shops use 37.5° per side = 75° included for extra room)
- **Land / root face:** 1/16" to 3/32" (1.6-2.4 mm)
- **Root gap:** 1/8" (3.2 mm) for 0.035" GMAW root, tighter for smaller wire
- **Tack welds:** 3-4 tacks equally spaced (12, 3, 6, 9 o'clock on a 5G pipe), feathered/ground flush before starting

**Bevel prep is typically done with:**
- Beveling machine (dedicated pipe beveler — cleanest, fastest)
- Grinder (portable, done by hand — most common in field work)
- Oxyfuel cutting torch (rough cut, then grind smooth)

---

## Numbers you need to memorize

- **1GR = 1G rolled** — pipe axis horizontal, rotated during welding[^3]
- **2G pipe** — pipe axis VERTICAL, weld runs horizontally around pipe (like a belt)[^3]
- **5G pipe** — pipe axis HORIZONTAL, pipe FIXED, welder progresses around it[^3]
- **6G pipe** — pipe axis at 45°, pipe fixed, hardest common position[^3]
- **GMAW root pass wire (downhill pipeline):** 0.035" ER70S-6[^1]
- **FCAW pipe fill/cap:** 0.045" E71T-1[^6]
- **Shielding gas for pipe GMAW root:** 75/25 Ar/CO2 or 100% CO2[^2]
- **Shielding gas for FCAW-G pipe fill/cap:** 75/25 Ar/CO2 (E71T-1 preferred mix)[^6]
- **All wire-feed pipe polarity:** DCEP[^1][^6]
- **Standard bevel:** 30° per side = 60° included angle (or 37.5° per side = 75° for extra room)[^4]
- **Standard root gap:** 1/8" (3.2 mm) for 0.035" GMAW short-arc root[^1]
- **Standard land:** 1/16" to 3/32" (1.6-2.4 mm)[^1]
- **Downhill root progression:** 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock[^1]
- **Uphill fill/cap progression:** 6 o'clock to 12 o'clock[^6]
- **Tack welds on 5G pipe:** typically 3-4 equally spaced, feathered/ground flush before start[^4]
- **5G amperage adjustment at 12 (overhead-ish):** reduce 10-15% below flat setting[^1]

---

## What the textbook doesn't tell you

**Every pipe weld starts with fit-up.** Root openings that vary by 1/32" around the pipe cause welders to fail X-ray tests. A well-fit joint is 80% of a good weld. Take the extra time with clamps, wedges, and tack sequence to get a uniform 1/8" gap all the way around. Fit-up is a real skill.[^4]

**Tacks matter more than you think.** A poorly-placed tack becomes a discontinuity when you weld over it. Standard practice: 4 tacks at 12/3/6/9 on a 5G pipe, each tack ~1/2" long, feathered on both ends with a grinder BEFORE starting the root pass. The root pass ties into the feathered tack invisibly.[^4]

**Downhill root technique feels wrong at first.** Coming from plate welding where uphill is standard, letting gravity pull the puddle down feels like it should cause burn-through. It doesn't — the short-arc + small puddle actually gives you MORE control because gravity keeps the puddle small. Trust the process, practice on scrap first.[^1][^5]

**5G at 6 o'clock is where welders fail.** As you descend, you're now welding in the flat position but with the puddle wanting to sag. Slow down at the transition (~5 o'clock), reduce amperage slightly, and be careful not to let the puddle grow. Overheated 6 o'clock = drop-through and failed test.[^1]

**Watch your gas coverage in wind.** Field pipe welding often has wind. GMAW/FCAW-G shielding gas gets stripped in > 10 km/h wind. Options: wind wall/tarp, pop-up shelter, or switch to processes that don't need external gas (SMAW E6010/E7018, or FCAW-S with E71T-11). Miss this and you get porosity throughout the weld.[^6]

**Machine settings for pipe are different from plate.** Wire feed speed (WFS) for GMAW pipe root is typically 250-350 IPM (inches per minute) with 0.035" wire. For FCAW pipe fill: 300-450 IPM with 0.045" wire. Match your WFS to the amperage/voltage combination your machine's chart recommends.[^1][^2]

**Pipe travel around the joint should be SMOOTH.** Sudden speed changes or arc stops leave visible starts/stops. Practice walking around the pipe smoothly — footwork, body positioning, cable management. A pipe welder who can dance around a 5G joint without breaking stride runs beautiful welds.[^1]

**Radiographic testing (X-ray) shows every mistake.** The most common defects on wire-feed pipe are: incomplete penetration at the root, wagon-track porosity (usually contamination), incomplete fusion at bevel walls, and inclusions at start/stop points. Each has a specific fix — but the best fix is to run clean the first time.[^5]

---

## Diagram

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p2-s5-c-pipe-positions.svg` — 4 pipe illustrations: 1GR rotating pipe, 2G vertical pipe with horizontal weld, 5G fixed horizontal pipe with weld progression arrows, 6G 45° pipe)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p2-s5-c-5g-progression.svg` — clock face on pipe showing welder progression from 12 to 3 to 6 (downhill) or 6 to 3 to 12 (uphill), with typical amperage/technique adjustments at each clock position)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p2-s5-c-pipe-joint-prep.svg` — cross-section of pipe joint prep: bevel angle labeled, land labeled, root gap labeled, with tack weld locations shown at 12/3/6/9 o'clock)*

---

## Key terms

- **1G / 1GR:** pipe horizontal, ROTATED (rolled) during welding — easiest pipe position
- **2G:** pipe vertical (axis vertical), weld horizontal around pipe
- **5G:** pipe horizontal, FIXED (welder walks around pipe)
- **6G:** pipe at 45°, fixed — hardest common position
- **Downhill:** weld progression from 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock (top to bottom)
- **Uphill:** weld progression from 6 o'clock to 12 o'clock (bottom to top)
- **1/2 stringer, 1/2 stringer pattern:** two-pass technique where one welder does one half, another does the other half
- **Walking the cup:** GTAW technique (not GMAW/FCAW) but often referenced in pipe welding culture
- **X-ray / RT (Radiographic Testing):** the standard acceptance test for critical pipe welds
- **Wagon-track porosity:** parallel lines of porosity on the sides of a weld (contamination indicator)

---

## Common exam trap

- **1GR = "1G rolled"** = horizontal pipe, ROTATED during welding. Not the same as 1G (fixed).
- **2G pipe** has pipe axis VERTICAL. Distractors may show pipe horizontal.
- **5G is FIXED** pipe (welder moves). 1G / 1GR is ROTATED pipe (pipe moves).
- **Downhill root pass on pipeline** is standard practice with GMAW short-arc. Distractors may say uphill is always required — that's for plate/refinery code work, not pipeline.
- **Bevel prep: 60° or 75° included** (30° or 37.5° per side). Not 45° included.
- **Tacks must be feathered before welding over them** to avoid discontinuity.
- **DCEP for all wire-feed pipe welding** with GMAW/FCAW-G/MCAW.
- **6G is the hardest common position** — every position at every angle. If you can pass 6G, you can weld any pipe joint.
- **Fit-up matters more than welding skill** — variable root gap = failed X-ray.

---

## Practice question preview

**Q:** A welder is preparing to run a 5G root pass on 6" schedule 40 mild steel pipe using GMAW with 0.035" ER70S-6. The joint is beveled to 60° included angle with a 1/16" land and 1/8" root gap. Four tack welds are in place at 12/3/6/9 o'clock positions. What should the welder do FIRST before striking the arc for the root pass?

A) Increase amperage 20% above normal 5G setting to burn through the tacks
B) Feather (grind smooth) both ends of each tack weld
C) Weld right over the tacks without modification
D) Remove all tacks and start from a fully open joint

**Correct: B**

**Explanation:** Tack welds must be feathered (ground smooth at both ends) before the root pass welds over them. Unmodified tacks become discontinuities where the root pass transitions from base metal to tack to base metal — creating an abrupt geometry change that causes lack of fusion, incomplete penetration, or wagon-track porosity at each tack location. A) Increasing amperage to burn through tacks causes over-penetration and root sag; C) Welding over unmodified tacks creates the exact defects that cause X-ray rejection; D) Removing tacks entirely leaves you without fit-up and the pipe will move as you weld.

**Red Seal mapping:** D-14.02 (Sets up FCAW, MCAW and GMAW equipment), D-14.04 (Performs weld using FCAW, MCAW and GMAW equipment)

---

[^2]: [Miller Electric — GMAW Pipe Welding Guide](https://www.millerwelds.com/resources/article-library/pipe-welding-basics); GMAW-P for pipe root passes, transfer mode selection for pipe

# Codes, Standards and Red Seal Certification

The difference between a journeyperson and a journeyperson who works in code shops is this: the journeyperson who works in code shops understands WHY the welds have to be done a certain way. Codes are not bureaucratic paperwork — they are the accumulated engineering judgement of what it takes to keep pressure vessels from exploding, bridges from collapsing, and pipelines from rupturing. When you understand the code system, you can work in any sector of the trade.

---

## Code, Standard, Specification — Three Different Things

These three words are used interchangeably in the field, but they mean different things to engineers:[^1][^2]

| Term | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | A legally enforceable set of requirements adopted by a jurisdiction (government body). Backed by law. | CSA B51 (provincial law in AB), ASME BPVC (adopted by AB Safety Codes Act) |
| **Standard** | A document produced by a consensus body (CSA, AWS, ASTM, ASME) that defines requirements. It becomes a code when adopted into law. | CSA W47.1, CSA W59, AWS D1.1 |
| **Specification** | A document that defines requirements for a specific material, product, or process in a specific project or contract. | A WPS (Welding Procedure Specification) for a specific pipe weld |

**Why it matters on the job:** When your foreman says "weld it to code," they mean the adopted standard applies. When they hand you a WPS, they're giving you a project-level specification. Both are binding.

---

## Who Sets the Standards? The Agencies

Each agency has a domain. Know which one owns which territory:[^1][^2][^3]

| Agency | Full Name | Main Domain |
|---|---|---|
| **CSA** | Canadian Standards Association | Canadian welding standards (W47.1, W59, B51, W117.2, W178.1) |
| **ASME** | American Society of Mechanical Engineers | Pressure vessels and pressure piping (BPVC, B31.3) |
| **AWS** | American Welding Society | Filler metal classifications (A5.x series), structural (D1.1), pipe (D1.1 ch. 9) |
| **API** | American Petroleum Institute | Petroleum pipeline (API 1104) and oil field equipment |
| **NBBI** | National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors | Inspection, repair, and re-rating of pressure vessels after initial code construction |
| **CGSB** | Canadian General Standards Board | NDT personnel certification (CGSB 48.9712) |
| **ASTM** | American Society for Testing and Materials | Material test methods (E8 tensile, E23 Charpy), material classifications (A36, A516 Gr. 70) |

---

## The Major Welding Codes — What They Govern

### CSA W47.1 — Company Certification for Welding[^1]

This is THE most important code for Alberta welders to understand. **CSA W47.1 certifies the COMPANY**, not the welder.

- **What it requires:**
  - A Certified Welding Engineer (CWE) or Engineer of Record must approve all WPS documents
  - The company must maintain qualified welders (tested to the WPS)
  - Quality control records must be kept
  - Third-party audits by CWB Group maintain certification
- **Who needs it:** Any company doing structural welding, pressure piping, or fabrication that will be inspected by a Safety Codes Officer in Alberta
- **Division structure:** Division 1 (complete certification), Division 2 (limited scope), Division 3 (on-site repair and maintenance)
- **As a welder:** When you work for a W47.1 company, your welder qualification cards are issued under that company's certification. If you leave, you may need to requalify at the new company — unless the new company accepts the same WPS scope.

### CSA W59 — Welded Steel Construction[^2]

Governs how steel structures (buildings, bridges, towers) are welded.

- **What it covers:**
  - Design of welded connections (throat size calculations, load types)
  - Workmanship (acceptable defect limits, interpass temperature, preheat by carbon equivalent)
  - Welder qualification positions and test requirements
  - Inspection requirements (VT, PT, MT, UT, RT criteria)
- **Key clauses welders use:**
  - Clause 4 (General requirements, preheat calculation by CE)
  - Clause 12 (Welder qualification — what positions qualify you for what)
  - Annex A (filler metal prequalification)
- **As a welder:** Your 3G plate test may qualify you for 1G and 3G production welds. W59 Clause 12 defines the qualification matrix exactly.

### CSA B51 — Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Pressure Piping Code[^1]

The provincial law that regulates all pressure-containing equipment in Alberta. It adopts ASME BPVC by reference.

- **Why it matters:** If the vessel holds compressed fluid — steam, process gas, hydraulic — B51 applies. Alberta's Safety Codes Act enforces B51.
- **As a welder:** You'll be welding to ASME BPVC Section IX (procedure and performance qualification), but the authority is B51. Your qualification documents must be traceable.

### ASME BPVC Section IX — Welding Qualifications[^3]

The most detailed qualification code in the industry. Used for pressure vessels, pressure piping, and anything adopted by ASME.

- **Part QW:** Welding (by far the most relevant part)
  - **QW-100 through QW-199:** General requirements and definitions
  - **QW-200 through QW-299:** Procedure qualification (PQR)
  - **QW-300 through QW-399:** Performance qualification (welder qualification)
  - **QW-400 through QW-499:** Essential and supplementary essential variables
  - **QW-500 through QW-599:** Filler metal classification and test requirements

### API 1104 — Welding of Pipelines[^2]

Used for cross-country petroleum pipeline welds.

- **Key difference from ASME:** API 1104 uses acceptance criteria based on radiographic testing of production welds (not just qualification coupons)
- **Pipeline root pass:** API 1104 allows and commonly uses E6010 downhill stringer bead root pass (unique to pipeline work)
- **As a welder:** Pipeline work typically requires you to qualify on API 1104 separately from your ASME or W47.1 cards

---

## Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and Procedure Qualification Record (PQR)

This is the heart of code welding. Every code weld must be backed by a documented procedure.[^1][^3]

### The three-document chain

```
PQR (test results) → supports → WPS (the instructions) → referenced by → Work Traveller/Blueprint (the job)
```

### WPS — Welding Procedure Specification

A WPS is a written document that instructs the welder how to make a specific weld. It must include:[^3]

| WPS element | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Base metal** | P-Number, Group Number, thickness range |
| **Filler metal** | F-Number, A-Number, AWS classification, diameter range |
| **Welding process** | SMAW, GTAW, FCAW, etc. |
| **Positions** | 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G, 5G, 6G |
| **Preheat and interpass temperature** | Min preheat °C, max interpass °C |
| **PWHT** | Temperature and time range (if required) |
| **Shielding gas** | Composition, flow rate range |
| **Electrical parameters** | Amperage, voltage, travel speed, polarity |
| **Joint design** | Bevel angle, root opening, backing |
| **Technique** | Stringer or weave, uphill or downhill |

**The welder FOLLOWS the WPS.** Deviating from the WPS — even if your instinct says otherwise — is a code violation. If the WPS is wrong, report it to the CWE. Don't change parameters on your own.

### PQR — Procedure Qualification Record

A PQR is the test record that proves the WPS parameters actually produce sound welds. It documents:[^3]

- The actual measured parameters during the test weld (amperage, voltage, travel speed)
- The test results (bend test, tensile test, radiographic examination)
- Signature of the testing agency or CWE who witnessed it

**The PQR certifies the procedure. The WPS certifies the instructions.** They must be consistent.

---

## Essential Variables vs Non-Essential Variables

When any essential variable changes, you need a new PQR and WPS (or a re-qualification test). Non-essential variables can be changed by amending the WPS without re-testing.[^3]

### Essential variables for welder performance qualification (ASME Section IX)[^3]

| Change | Essential? |
|---|---|
| Process change (SMAW → GTAW) | YES — new test required |
| Position change (1G → 3G) | YES (going to harder position requires test in that position) |
| Filler metal F-Number change | YES |
| Backing removal (with backing → open root) | YES |
| Polarity change (DCEP → DCEN) | YES |
| Electrical characteristic (AC → DC) | YES |

### Non-essential variables (can change without re-test)

| Change | Non-essential? |
|---|---|
| Amperage within qualified range | YES |
| Travel speed adjustment within range | YES |
| Joint design changes | YES (within prequalified limits) |
| Pass sequence (stringer vs weave) | YES |
| Preheat temperature increase | YES (decrease may be essential) |

**Exam trap:** Adding backing (going from open root to backed joint) is generally NOT essential for a welder qualification — it makes the joint EASIER. Removing backing IS essential — it makes the joint harder.

---

## Welder Performance Qualification

When you do a qualification test, here's what you're proving — and what it buys you:[^1][^3]

### Qualification test coupon → production positions covered

Under ASME Section IX QW-303 and CSA W47.1 Annex B:[^1][^3]

| Test coupon | Production positions qualified |
|---|---|
| 1G plate (flat) | 1G only |
| 2G plate (horizontal) | 1G, 2G |
| 3G plate (vertical up) | 1G, 3G |
| 4G plate (overhead) | 1G, 4G |
| 3G + 4G plate combination | 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G (all positions on plate) |
| 6G pipe (inclined, rotated) | All pipe positions (2G, 5G, 6G) AND all plate positions |

**The 6G is the gold standard qualification.** It qualifies you for everything. Pipeline companies and pressure vessel shops often require a 6G for employment.

### How long does a qualification last?

Under ASME Section IX QW-322:[^3]

- Qualification is valid as long as you weld in that process at least **once every 6 months**
- If you don't weld in the process for 6+ months, your qualification expires and you must re-test
- Medical incapacitation with supervisor documentation may extend this

---

## Carbon Equivalent and Preheat — Code Requirement

CSA W59 Annex A requires preheat based on the carbon equivalent (CE) of the steel.[^2]

### Carbon equivalent formula (IIW method)

**CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15**[^2]

Where all values are weight % from the mill test report.

| CE Range | Preheat required (CSA W59) |
|---|---|
| CE < 0.35 | None required (for t < 25 mm) |
| CE 0.35 – 0.55 | Min preheat 93 °C (200 °F) |
| CE > 0.55 | Min preheat 150 °C (300 °F) or per engineering |

**Read the mill test report (MTR) before you strike an arc.** The CE is calculated from the chemistry shown on the MTR. If CE > 0.35 and you don't preheat, you risk hydrogen cracking in the HAZ — and the weld fails inspection.

---

## Using the RSOS to Prepare for Red Seal

The Red Seal Occupational Standard (RSOS) is your exam blueprint.[^5]

### RSOS structure

```
Blocks (MWA) → Tasks → Sub-tasks → Performance Criteria
```

- **Block A** (Common Occupational Skills) — 16% of exam, 20 questions
- **Block B** (Layout and Fabrication) — 22% of exam, 28 questions
- **Block C** (Cutting and Gouging) — 18% of exam, 23 questions
- **Block D** (Welding Processes) — 44% of exam, 54 questions

### How to use the RSOS for studying

1. **Download the RSOS PDF** from red-seal.ca — it's free
2. Every sub-task (e.g., D-13.04 "Performs weld using SMAW equipment") lists performance criteria that exam questions are written from
3. For each sub-task, ask yourself: "Could someone write a multiple-choice question about this criterion? What would the wrong answers look like?"
4. Pay attention to the **"common core" indicator** — common core sub-tasks are tested in every jurisdiction. Alberta-specific tasks are also tested but weighted differently in some jurisdictions.

**The Red Seal exam has 125 questions. You need 88 correct (70%) to pass.** Block D (Welding Processes) has 54 questions — if you're weak there, fix it first.

---

## Numbers you need to memorize

- **Red Seal exam:** 125 questions, 4 hours, 70% pass mark (88 correct)[^5]
- **Period exam pass mark:** 70%[^5]
- **ASME Section IX minimum test coupon thickness:** 3/8" (9.5 mm) for groove welds unless using thinner parent material[^3]
- **Welder qualification expiry:** 6 months without process use, per ASME QW-322[^3]
- **CE < 0.35:** No preheat required for t < 25 mm (W59)[^2]
- **CE 0.35–0.55:** Min preheat 93 °C (200 °F)[^2]
- **CE > 0.55:** Min preheat 150 °C (300 °F)[^2]
- **6G pipe qualification:** qualifies all pipe AND plate positions[^1][^3]
- **3G + 4G plate combination:** qualifies all plate positions[^1]

---

## What the textbook doesn't tell you

**Your qualification cards are portable, but your WPS coverage isn't.** The card says you passed a 3G test. The WPS says the joint geometry, filler metal, and material limits. When you move to a new company, check that their WPS scope matches what you've qualified on — you may need a new test coupon on their materials.[^1]

**Pipeline companies run their own qualification tests regardless of your existing cards.** Even if you have a 6G ASME card, a pipeline company will make you run a test coupon on their pipe, to their WPS, witnessed by their welding inspector. This is normal and expected.[^2]

**The WPS is a living document.** Engineering changes, base metal substitutions, filler metal changes — all require WPS revisions and PQR re-confirmation. If you're handed a WPS dated 2015 and the job is using 2024 material grades, ask if the WPS has been updated.[^3]

**"Prequalified" WPS (CSA W47.1 Annex D / AWS D1.1 Annex B):** Some joints are so standard that they don't require a PQR test — the code prequalifies them. Conditions are strict (specific filler metals, joint geometry, process combinations). Your company may use prequalified WPS for standard structural work, saving the cost of test coupons.[^1]

**The CGSB NDT certification is separate from your welder qualification.** The person interpreting your radiographs, doing your UT, or reading your PT is a CGSB-certified inspector. As a welder, you should understand what they're looking for — it makes you a better first-pass inspector of your own work.[^4]

---

## Diagram

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-a-code-hierarchy.svg` — pyramid diagram showing law at top, code at second level (CSA B51, ASME BPVC adopted), standard at third level (CSA W47.1, W59, AWS D1.1), specification at base (WPS, PQR) — with arrows showing adoption/reference flow)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-a-wps-pqr-chain.svg` — three-box flow diagram: PQR test record → supports → WPS written document → referenced by → Work Traveller/Job Card)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-a-qualification-matrix.svg` — table showing coupon position tested vs production positions covered, with 6G at the top covering all)*

---

## Key terms

- **Code:** A legally enforceable set of requirements adopted by a jurisdiction
- **Standard:** A consensus document that defines requirements; becomes a code when adopted by law
- **Specification:** A project-level document defining requirements for a specific item
- **WPS (Welding Procedure Specification):** Written instructions for making a specific weld
- **PQR (Procedure Qualification Record):** Test record that validates the WPS parameters
- **Essential variable:** A parameter change that requires a new PQR test
- **Non-essential variable:** A parameter change that requires only a WPS amendment
- **Carbon equivalent (CE):** A formula relating steel chemistry to hardenability and preheat requirement
- **6G:** The inclined rotated pipe position — the highest qualification, covers all positions
- **CWE:** Certified Welding Engineer — must approve WPS documents under W47.1
- **CWB Group:** Canadian Welding Bureau — third-party auditor for W47.1 certification
- **MAWP:** Maximum Allowable Working Pressure — a design parameter on pressure vessels
- **MTR / MTC:** Mill Test Report / Mill Test Certificate — the chemistry and mechanical properties of the plate/pipe as delivered from the steel mill

---

## Common exam trap

- **"Code" and "standard" are NOT the same thing.** A code is law. A standard is adopted into law to become a code. Exam questions will try to reverse these definitions.
- **CSA W47.1 certifies the COMPANY, not the individual welder.** Questions may ask "what does W47.1 certify?" — the answer is the company's welding operations, not the welder personally.
- **Adding backing = easier test (NOT essential variable).** Removing backing = harder test (IS essential). Don't flip these.
- **The 3G coupon alone qualifies you for 1G and 3G only — NOT 2G or 4G.** Need 3G + 4G (or 2G + 3G + 4G) for full plate coverage.
- **Welder qualification expires after 6 months without process use** — not 3 months, not 1 year.
- **ASME Section IX, CSA W47.1, and AWS D1.1 have DIFFERENT qualification matrices.** A weld position that qualifies you for more positions under one code may be more restrictive under another. Always check which code applies.
- **CE formula:** C + Mn/6 + (Cr+Mo+V)/5 + (Ni+Cu)/15 — memorize the denominators (6, 5, 15). They will put 3, 5, 6 in the wrong places.

---

## Practice question preview

**Q:** A welder has a valid ASME Section IX 3G plate qualification but has not performed any SMAW welding for 8 months. Which of the following best describes the welder's qualification status?

A) Still valid — plate qualifications do not expire  
B) Expired — the welder must re-test on a 3G coupon  
C) Suspended — the welder must submit documentation to ASME  
D) Valid for 6 more months after submitting an extension request

**Correct: B**

**Explanation:** ASME Section IX QW-322 states that a welder's qualification expires if they have not welded with that process in any 6-month period. 8 months exceeds this limit. The welder must run a new test coupon to re-establish qualification. There is no "suspension" status or extension request mechanism in QW-322 — the qualification simply lapses and requires re-testing.

**Red Seal mapping:** A-4.01 (Uses documentation and reference material)

---

[^1]: [CSA W47.1 — Certification of Companies for Fusion Welding of Steel](https://www.csagroup.org/store/product/CSA%20W47%3A1/); Clause 4 (Engineer of Record duties), Clause 8 (WPS requirements), Clause 9 (Welder qualification matrix), Annex B (qualification scope)
[^2]: [CSA W59 — Welded Steel Construction (2018)](https://www.csagroup.org/store/product/CSA%20W59%3A18/); Clause 4 (preheat by carbon equivalent, Annex A CE formula), Clause 12 (welder qualification positions), Annex A (prequalified filler metals)
[^3]: [ASME BPVC Section IX — Welding, Brazing, and Fusing Qualifications](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/find-codes-standards/bpvc-ix-boiler-pressure-vessel-code-section-ix-welding-brazing); QW-100 (general), QW-200 (procedure qualification), QW-300 (performance qualification), QW-322 (expiry of qualification), QW-400 (essential variables)
[^4]: [CSA W178.1 — Certification of Welding Inspection Organizations](https://www.csagroup.org/store/product/CSA%20W178%3A1/); Clause 4 (organization requirements), Clause 5 (inspector qualification levels)

  - source: Victor Technologies (ESAB) — Oxy-Fuel Equipment Operating Instructions
    ref: Bevel cutting setup, piercing technique, tip sizes and pressure tables
    url: https://www.esab.com/globalassets/products/equipment/cutting/oxyfuel/operating-manual.pdf
  - source: CSA W117.2 — Safety in Welding, Cutting, and Allied Processes
    ref: Clause 9 (gas welding and cutting safety), Clause 10 (fire prevention), PPE requirements
    url: https://www.csagroup.org/store/product/CSA%20W117%3A2/

    ref: Section 5 (hot work permits), Section 6 (fire watch requirements), Section 8 (PPE)
    url: https://www.nfpa.org/codes-and-standards/all-codes-and-standards/list-of-codes-and-standards/detail?code=51B

    ref: Preheat flame adjustment, cutting speed, plate thickness parameters
    url: https://www.lincolnelectric.com/en/education-center/welding-education

# Oxyfuel Cutting on Mild Steel — Advanced Techniques

Every fabrication shop runs an oxyfuel torch. It costs almost nothing per cut on heavy steel, it can reach where plasma cannot, and it's the only process that reliably bevels 4-inch plate for groove weld prep without specialized CNC equipment. Period 3 oxyfuel is not "light it and cut" — it's bevel cutting, piercing holes in plate, and coping structural shapes. These skills separate fabricators from fitters.

---

## How Oxyfuel Cutting Actually Works — The Chemistry

Oxyfuel cutting is not melting. It's **oxidation** (rapid burning).[^1]

The process has two distinct phases:

1. **Preheat:** The preheat flame (acetylene or propane with oxygen) brings the steel to its **kindling temperature** — approximately 870–980 °C (1600–1800 °F) for mild steel. At this temperature, steel glows bright orange.

2. **Cutting:** A high-pressure stream of **pure oxygen** is released through the cutting orifice. At kindling temperature, mild steel burns (oxidizes) in pure oxygen. The iron oxide formed is a liquid that is blown out of the cut by the oxygen jet pressure.

**Why it only works on mild steel and low-alloy steels:**
- The melting point of iron oxide (FeO) is LOWER than the melting point of the steel. The oxide liquefies and gets blown clear.
- In stainless steel, chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃) has a HIGHER melting point than the steel itself — it forms a solid crust that blocks the oxygen stream. Oxyfuel cutting does NOT work on stainless without flux injection.[^1]
- Cast iron has too much carbon — the preheat flame dissolves the carbon into the gas before oxidation can proceed. Plasma cutting is used instead.

---

## Gases and Their Characteristics

| Gas | Max fuel-to-oxygen ratio | Flame temp (°C) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acetylene (C₂H₂)** | 1:1.2–1.5 (cutting) | ~3100 | Hottest, fastest preheat, primary preheat flame. Unstable above 103 kPa (15 psi). [^1] |
| **Propane (C₃H₈)** | 1:4.5 (cutting) | ~2850 | Slower preheat, cooler flame, denser than air (sinks to floor). Cheaper per GJ. |
| **Natural gas (CH₄)** | 1:1.5–2.0 (cutting) | ~2770 | Lowest flame temp, slowest preheat. Used on automated CNC tables. |
| **MAPP Gas (withdrawn)** | Similar to propane | ~2900 | Discontinued commercially; propylene blends used instead |

**Acetylene rule:** NEVER exceed 103 kPa (15 psi) gauge pressure at the torch. Above 103 kPa, acetylene becomes shock-sensitive and can decompose explosively without external ignition.[^3]

**Propane rule:** Propane is heavier than air. In confined spaces, propane leaks pool at floor level and create explosion hazards. Adequate ventilation means air movement at floor level, not just at head height.[^3]

---

## Tip Selection — The Critical Variable

The cutting tip (nozzle) is sized for the material thickness. Using the wrong tip is the most common cause of poor cuts.[^1][^2]

### General acetylene cutting tip size guide (approximate)[^2]

| Steel thickness | Tip size (approx) | O₂ cutting pressure (kPa / psi) | Fuel pressure (kPa / psi) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3–6 mm (1/8–1/4") | #000 – #0 | 175–241 kPa (25–35 psi) | 7–14 kPa (1–2 psi) |
| 6–12 mm (1/4–1/2") | #0 – #1 | 207–276 kPa (30–40 psi) | 7–21 kPa (1–3 psi) |
| 12–25 mm (1/2–1") | #1 – #2 | 241–310 kPa (35–45 psi) | 14–28 kPa (2–4 psi) |
| 25–50 mm (1–2") | #2 – #3 | 276–345 kPa (40–50 psi) | 21–34 kPa (3–5 psi) |
| 50–100 mm (2–4") | #3 – #4 | 310–414 kPa (45–60 psi) | 28–48 kPa (4–7 psi) |

*Note: Always verify exact pressures with the torch manufacturer's tip chart — different manufacturers have different orifice sizes for the "same" tip number.[^2]*

### Signs of wrong tip or pressure setting

| Problem | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Cut face has deep drag lines (lag) | Travel too fast OR oxygen pressure too low OR tip too small |
| Cut face is rounded at top, undercut | Too slow OR oxygen pressure too high |
| Preheat cones are too long or luminous | Too much acetylene (rich flame) |
| Cut stops mid-piece | Tip clogging OR plate too thick for tip |
| Excessive slag that won't knock off | Travel speed too slow OR low carbon steel correct, but slag is normal for thick steel |

---

## Flame Adjustment — Getting the Neutral Flame

Before cutting, the preheat flame must be properly adjusted.[^1][^2]

### Acetylene flame types

1. **Carbonizing (rich) flame:** excess acetylene — three-cone structure (luminous inner cone, intermediate feather, outer envelope). Carbon deposits on steel. Wrong for cutting.

2. **Neutral flame:** oxygen-to-acetylene ratio balanced — two-cone structure (sharp inner cone, transparent outer envelope). No carbon deposit. Correct for most steel cutting and welding.

3. **Oxidizing flame:** excess oxygen — single sharp cone, slightly purple tinge. Short inner cone. Burns hotter than neutral. Can be used for cutting but oxidizes the steel surface during preheat, creating mill-scale-like crust.

**For oxyfuel cutting, set a slightly oxidizing to neutral preheat flame.** A true neutral prevents carbon pickup during preheat.[^1]

### Lighting and adjusting procedure
1. Crack the oxygen valve slightly
2. Open the fuel valve, ignite with friction lighter (NEVER a match or lighter — back-flash risk)
3. Adjust fuel until the carbonizing feather disappears (at neutral)
4. For propane: adjust until the inner cone is sharp and blue
5. Test cutting oxygen — flame should increase slightly in size without going out

---

## Straight Cutting Technique (Reviewed from P1/P2)

- **Standoff distance:** 6–10 mm (1/4–3/8") from tip to plate surface (for acetylene tips without a stand-off guide).[^1] Too close = tip clogging. Too far = preheat is diffuse, slow, and cut quality suffers.
- **Torch angle:** typically 0° (perpendicular to plate surface) for a straight cut
- **Travel speed:** found by watching the cut. Proper speed = sparks (slag) blow downward and slightly ahead of the cut. Too fast = sparks blow backward. Too slow = slag stacks up on the bottom edge.
- **Start:** begin at the edge of the plate if possible. If you must start in the middle, pierce first (see below).

---

## Bevel Cutting — The Period 3 Core Skill

Bevel cutting produces an angled face on the plate edge for groove weld preparation. Every structural and pressure vessel groove weld starts with a beveled edge.[^1][^2]

### Setup for bevel cutting

1. **Mark the cut line:** use soapstone on the plate face, or a scribed line on the surface
2. **Determine the bevel angle:** typical groove prep angles are 22.5° per side (45° included) or 30° per side (60° included). For a single-V bevel, one side is cut.
3. **Tilt the torch:** angle the torch away from vertical by the bevel angle. If cutting a 30° bevel, tilt the torch 30° from vertical (60° from the plate surface).
4. **Use a guide:** a bevel cutting guide (a small wheeled jig that clamps on the torch and rides on the plate surface) is highly recommended for straight, consistent bevels. Without a guide, it takes significant practice to hold a consistent angle over 1–3 metre cuts.
5. **Maintain standoff:** with a guide wheel, standoff is set by the guide. Without a guide, maintain a consistent 6–10 mm tip-to-surface distance.

### Bevel angle measurement

The bevel angle is measured from the vertical (90°) of the plate edge:
- **30° bevel:** 30° from vertical = 60° from the plate surface
- **22.5° bevel:** 22.5° from vertical = 67.5° from the plate surface

**Check with a bevel protractor** after cutting. The bevel angle must be within ±2.5° for most code applications.[^2]

### Root face (land)

After bevel cutting, the bottom of the bevel has a small flat area — the root face or land. For oxyfuel-cut bevels, this is typically 1.5–3 mm (1/16–1/8"). If it's too large, it can be ground down. If the bevel cuts all the way to a sharp knife edge, a slight grinding step creates the land.[^1]

### Multi-pass beveling on thick plate

For plate > 50 mm (2 inches), a single-pass bevel cut can be difficult because:
- The oxygen jet has trouble reaching the root of the cut when highly angled
- The preheat may not fully penetrate to the bottom of the cut at high angles

**Two-pass method:** Make a roughing cut first (close to the final angle, leaving 3–5 mm material), then a finishing pass at the exact angle. Or make a straight cut first to remove the bulk of the material, then tilt the torch for the bevel in a second pass.[^2]

---

## Piercing — Starting a Cut in the Middle of a Plate

Piercing is required when you cannot start at the edge — for example, cutting a hole for a pipe nozzle in a vessel shell, or starting a cut-out in the middle of a floor plate.[^1]

### Piercing procedure

1. **Preheat the spot** with the preheat flame at a slight angle (about 5–10° from perpendicular) until the spot glows bright orange (870–980 °C)
2. **Increase standoff** distance to 20–25 mm (3/4–1") before opening the cutting oxygen — this prevents the blow-back of molten iron oxide from clogging the tip
3. **Open the cutting oxygen slowly:** the steel will begin to oxidize. You'll see a shower of sparks below and orange slag blowing upward.
4. **Lower the torch gradually** as the cut penetrates — slowly bring it back to normal standoff once the jet has cut through
5. **Resume normal travel speed** once the pierce is complete

### Pierce hazards[^3]

- **Blow-back:** molten slag is ejected upward during piercing. ALWAYS position your body to the side, NOT directly above or in the path of the ejected slag.
- **Spatter damage:** cover nearby equipment and instrumentation with fire-resistant blankets before piercing
- **Fire watch required:** sparks can travel 10 m (33 ft) or more. A second person as fire watch is required per NFPA 51B Section 6 during confined space or elevated work.[^4]

---

## Coping — Cutting Structural Shapes

Coping is the removal of material from the end of a structural shape (I-beam, channel, angle) so it can fit against another member. A coped W-section looks like a notch cut at the end of the flange and web.[^1]

### Why cope?

- An I-beam connecting to another beam web needs its top and bottom flanges cut back so only the web passes through (or butts against the web)
- Coping prevents flange-to-flange interference in beam connections
- Calculated precisely: the cope depth and length are shown on structural drawings

### Coping procedure

1. **Lay out the cope:** measure and mark with soapstone. Mark both sides of the beam web for reference.
2. **Determine sequence:** typically cut the flange first (straight cut at the cope depth), then cut the web vertical face (to the cope length).
3. **Cut the flange:** straight cut perpendicular to the beam axis, at the cope depth. Cut from the flange edge toward the web.
4. **Stop at the fillet radius:** the junction of the web and flange has a fillet. Do NOT try to cut the fillet sharp — leave a 6–10 mm radius and remove the remnant with an angle grinder. A sharp notch in the cope creates a stress concentration.
5. **Cut the web face:** straight cut parallel to the beam axis, at the cope length. Cut from the preheat flame through the web.
6. **Grind smooth:** all cope cuts should be ground smooth with an angle grinder. Burrs, gouges, and roughness at cope edges concentrate stress.

**Common structural cope dimensions (typical — verify against structural drawings):**
- Cope depth: 1.5× flange thickness, or as drawn
- Cope length: 1.5× d (beam depth), or as drawn
- Corner radius: 25 mm (1") minimum per CISC Handbook practice[^1]

---

## Quality Checks on Oxyfuel Cuts

A well-made oxyfuel cut has these characteristics:[^1][^2]

| Quality indicator | Acceptable | Reject |
|---|---|---|
| **Drag lines** | Nearly vertical (slight rearward lean acceptable) | Steeply angled backward (too fast) |
| **Cut face** | Smooth, consistent | Deep gouges, washout, slag islands |
| **Top edge** | Sharp, slight rounding acceptable | Melted round edge (too slow or too close) |
| **Bottom edge** | Minimal slag | Thick, solidified slag not removable with chipping hammer |
| **Bevel angle** | Within ±2.5° | Varies > 2.5° along cut length |
| **Squareness** | Both faces perpendicular to each other ± 2° | Twisted bevel |

---

## Numbers you need to memorize

- **Acetylene max pressure:** 103 kPa (15 psi) — NEVER exceed[^3]
- **Kindling temperature for mild steel:** 870–980 °C (1600–1800 °F)[^1]
- **Normal standoff distance:** 6–10 mm (1/4–3/8") from tip to plate[^1]
- **Pierce standoff distance:** 20–25 mm (3/4–1") before opening cutting oxygen[^1]
- **Acetylene flame temp:** ~3100 °C (hottest common fuel gas)[^1]
- **Propane flame temp:** ~2850 °C[^1]
- **Bevel angle tolerance:** ±2.5° for most code applications[^2]
- **Cope corner radius minimum:** 25 mm (1") per CISC practice[^1]
- **Fire watch travel distance:** sparks can travel 10 m (33 ft) or more[^4]

---

## What the textbook doesn't tell you

**You CANNOT make a good bevel cut without a guide on long cuts.** Hand-holding a torch at 30° for 3 metres and maintaining a consistent angle is a skill that takes months to develop. Get a guide wheel or a circle cutting attachment. If your company doesn't have one, ask — they cost less than one hour of welder time wasted on a bad bevel.[^2]

**Slag sticking to the bottom is a cut quality indicator, not a cleaning problem.** If your slag is hard to remove with a hammer, you were too slow. Fast cuts produce slag that falls away cleanly or drops with one hammer tap.[^1]

**Propane users: make sure you're adjusting for the different flame chemistry.** Propane requires much more oxygen than acetylene (4.5:1 ratio vs 1.2:1). The torch setup for propane is different from acetylene — the fuel-oxygen mixing is different, the tip orifices are sized differently, and the pressures are different. Never swap an acetylene tip into a propane torch without verifying it's compatible.[^1]

**The pierce blow-back will surprise you the first time.** The shower of orange-hot slag coming back at your face is alarming. Always wear a full-face shield (not just goggles), position your body to the side, and never pierce directly above your head or hands. Shield nearby equipment with a fire blanket.[^3]

**Cut quality on thick plate deteriorates with dirty tips.** Clean tips before EVERY cutting session with tip cleaners (spiral-flute files). Do not use drills — they enlarge the orifice and ruin the tip. A clean tip makes a straight, square cut; a dirty tip makes a wandering, undercut mess.[^2]

---

## Diagram

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-b-bevel-cut-setup.svg` — side view showing torch tilted at bevel angle relative to vertical plate, annotated with: tip standoff, bevel angle (from vertical), root face/land, cutting direction)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-b-pierce-sequence.svg` — three-step sequence: step 1 preheat at angle with increased standoff, step 2 open cutting oxygen while tilted, step 3 lower to normal standoff and travel. Arrows showing slag blow-back direction.)*

*(SVG to be added: `assets/diagrams/p3-s1-b-cope-geometry.svg` — end view of W-section beam showing cope cuts: flange cut depth, web face cut length, corner radius, before/after comparison)*

---

## Key terms

- **Kindling temperature:** the temperature at which steel ignites in pure oxygen (~870–980 °C for mild steel)
- **Oxidation:** the chemical reaction between iron and pure oxygen at kindling temperature — this IS the cut
- **Drag lines:** the striations left on the cut face showing the path of the oxygen jet through the steel
- **Standoff distance:** the distance between the torch tip and the plate surface
- **Root face / land:** the flat bottom portion of a beveled edge, retained to control root gap
- **Bevel angle:** the angle of the cut face measured from the vertical of the plate edge
- **Pierce:** starting a cut in the middle of the plate (not from an edge)
- **Cope:** removing material from the end of a structural shape to allow it to fit against another member
- **Fillet radius:** the inside curved transition between the flange and web of a structural shape — must not be notched sharply when coping
- **Drag:** the rearward lean of the cut face — acceptable when slight, indicates too-fast travel when excessive

---

## Common exam trap

- **Acetylene MAX pressure is 103 kPa (15 psi).** Exam questions often offer 207 kPa (30 psi) or 138 kPa (20 psi) as distractors. Always 103 kPa / 15 psi.
- **Oxyfuel cutting = oxidation, NOT melting.** Exam questions may describe it as "melting the steel." The correct term is oxidizing (burning) the steel in a pure oxygen jet.
- **Propane sinks; acetylene is slightly lighter than air.** In confined space, propane pools at floor level. Acetylene diffuses upward. Questions may ask about safe ventilation placement.
- **Pierce position:** stand to the SIDE, not above. Slag blows upward and backward during piercing.
- **Cope corner MUST have a radius** — not a sharp notch. Stress concentration causes fatigue cracking in service.
- **Stainless steel CANNOT be cut with standard oxyfuel.** The chromium oxide film blocks the cut. Use plasma cutting instead.

---

## Practice question preview

**Q:** A welder is piercing a 25 mm (1") hole in the middle of a mild steel plate to start a cut-out. Before opening the cutting oxygen lever, what should the welder do with the torch standoff distance compared to normal cutting?

A) Decrease it to 3 mm to concentrate heat  
B) Keep it at the normal 6–10 mm — no change needed  
C) Increase it to 20–25 mm to prevent slag blow-back onto the tip  
D) Move to 50 mm and use maximum oxygen pressure to force the pierce

**Correct: C**

**Explanation:** During piercing, the molten iron oxide is ejected upward (back toward the torch) when the oxygen jet first breaks through. Increasing standoff to 20–25 mm keeps the tip above the blow-back zone. If you pierce at normal standoff (6–10 mm), the ejected slag will clog the tip orifices immediately, requiring tip cleaning before the cut can continue. D is wrong — 50 mm is too far and the preheat is too diffuse.

**Red Seal mapping:** C-10.04 (Performs cut and gouge using OFC equipment)

---

# Workplace Coaching Skills

When you get your journeyperson ticket, your job changes. You're no longer just a welder — you're responsible for the apprentice working beside you. The quality of their training is in your hands. Most journeypersons were never taught how to teach; they just got shown things by someone who also wasn't taught how to teach. This lesson breaks the cycle.

---

## Why This Matters — Legal and Practical

Under Alberta's Apprenticeship and Industry Training Act, a certified journeyperson working with an apprentice has specific obligations:[^2]

- **Provide adequate supervision:** you must be in a position to observe the apprentice's work and intervene if safety is at risk
- **Ensure the apprentice is performing work relevant to the trade:** an apprentice should be doing welding work, not exclusively running errands or moving material
- **Sign off on the Record of Training:** your signature on the apprentice's record book is a legal statement that they performed and demonstrated the listed competencies

Beyond the law: **how you coach directly determines whether the apprentice becomes a competent welder or a dangerous one.** The industry needs qualified welders. The fastest path is a journeyperson who can actually teach.

---

## The Four-Step Coaching Model

The most effective approach to on-the-job training follows a structured four-step cycle.[^3]

### Step 1 — Set Expectations

Before the apprentice touches any equipment:

- **Explain the task clearly:** "Today we're going to practice running the root pass on a 3G V-groove. The goal is consistent penetration with no burn-through."
- **State the standard:** "A good root pass has a slightly raised crown on the back side — about 1/16" maximum — and no undercut or cold lap at the toes."
- **Explain the safety requirements:** "Before we start, here's the PPE: full leather sleeves, shade 10 lens minimum. Keep your body to the side of the weld axis — flash burns through your sleeve if you're directly over the arc."
- **Explain what you'll be observing:** "I'm going to watch your body position, arc length, travel speed, and the sound of the arc. I'll let you run the whole pass before I give feedback."

**Why setting expectations works:** apprentices who know exactly what "good" looks like before they start are better self-monitors during the task.[^3]

### Step 2 — Demonstrate

Show the task before asking the apprentice to do it:[^1][^3]

- **Demonstrate at real speed first:** run the root pass at normal production speed. Let them see what the finished product looks like.
- **Demonstrate at slow speed with narration:** run through the key movements while talking out loud. "Watch how I hold the electrode angle — 10–15° toward the direction of travel — and listen to the arc sound. That's the sound of a correct arc length."
- **Show the checkpoints:** after the pass, show the back-side penetration bead, the cross-section if grinding is needed, and what a defect looks like vs. what an acceptable bead looks like.
- **Invite questions before the apprentice starts:** "Any questions about what you just saw? What's the first thing you're going to focus on when you start?"

### Step 3 — Observe

Let the apprentice do the task while you watch — without interrupting unless there's a safety issue:[^3]

- **Stand where you can see both the arc and the apprentice's body position**
- **Watch for:** electrode angle drift, arc length changes (audible — too long sounds like crackling, correct sounds smooth and steady), puddle control, travel speed consistency, body position
- **Take notes mentally** (or on a card) of what went well and what needs improvement
- **Do NOT correct mid-task** unless:
  - Safety is at risk (flash, fire, crush)
  - The error will compound and make the coupon unsalvageable (e.g., running way too fast and creating a cold joint that will fail)
  - The apprentice asks you to stop

**Why observe without interrupting:** constant correction during the task prevents the apprentice from developing self-monitoring. They become dependent on the journeyperson's voice instead of their own senses.[^3]

### Step 4 — Provide Feedback

Structured feedback after the task is the most powerful tool you have.[^1][^3]

#### The feedback sequence

1. **Ask first:** "How do you think that went? What felt right? What felt off?"
   - This develops self-assessment — the most important skill for a welder working alone
   - Often the apprentice already knows what they did wrong

2. **Reinforce the specific things that were correct:** "Your electrode angle was rock-solid for the first half. That's where I want to see it every pass."
   - Be specific — not "good job" — the apprentice needs to know WHICH behaviors to repeat

3. **Identify the one most important thing to improve:** "The one thing I want you to work on next time: arc length. When you speeded up in the middle, your arc stretched out. Listen for that crackling sound — that's your signal to close up."
   - One improvement point at a time. Giving 5 things to fix at once is overwhelming and produces no change.

4. **Demonstrate the corrected behavior:** if the correction is technical, show it again immediately while describing it

5. **Have them try again:** repeat the cycle immediately with the correction in mind

#### Feedback language matters

| Instead of... | Say... |
|---|---|
| "You're doing it wrong" | "Here's what I noticed — try this adjustment" |
| "That's terrible" | "The root is cold at the start — let's look at why" |
| "Watch me again" | "Let me show you what a correct arc length looks like" |
| "You're not listening" | "Let me explain this differently — here's what's happening physically" |

---

## Safety Oversight — Non-Negotiable

As a journeyperson coaching an apprentice, your first responsibility is safety:[^4]

- **PPE verification:** check that the apprentice is fully geared (correct shade lens, gloves, sleeves, footwear) BEFORE they strike an arc
- **Confined space:** never let an apprentice work in a confined space without a trained entry supervisor present — this is not a task to practice with a new apprentice unless you are a trained confined space entry supervisor yourself
- **Hot work permits:** if the shop requires a hot work permit, the apprentice must see you complete it — learning permit compliance is part of the apprenticeship
- **Immediate stop authority:** if you observe any unsafe act, stop the work immediately, explain the hazard, and correct it before proceeding. This is both your right and your obligation under the OHS Act.

---

## Giving Feedback on Safety Violations

Safety feedback must be direct and immediate — this is the one time you DO interrupt:[^4]

- **Stop the work:** "Stop. Put down the electrode."
- **State the hazard:** "You don't have your gloves on and you're holding that hot metal."
- **Correct it:** "Put on your gloves. Always. No exceptions."
- **Explain the consequence:** "A burn to your hand can put you off work for weeks. The gloves are there for a reason."
- **Check understanding:** "What are you going to do differently every time from here on?"

Never make safety feedback personal — it's about the behavior, not the person.

---

## Numbers you need to memorize

- **Alberta journeyperson-to-apprentice ratio:** 1:1 mandatory supervision for first-period apprentices (verify current AIT regulations — ratios may vary by employer permit)[^2]
- **Feedback principle:** one improvement point at a time — not five[^3]
- **Feedback sequence:** Ask → Reinforce specific positives → One improvement → Demonstrate → Repeat[^3]

---

## What the textbook doesn't tell you

**Patience is a skill, not a personality trait.** Good coaches are not born patient — they practice restraint. Every time you resist grabbing the electrode out of the apprentice's hand and doing it yourself, you're building their competence and your coaching skill simultaneously.[^3]

**Show-and-tell beats tell-only every time.** Telling an apprentice that their arc length is wrong has almost no effect. Showing them what the weld bead looks like when the arc is too long — and then what it looks like correct — fixes the problem in one session.[^1]

**Journal your observations.** After coaching sessions, a brief note on what the apprentice did well and what needs work helps you track progress over weeks. "Improved arc length consistency since last Tuesday" is useful feedback context. Without notes, it's easy to focus on the same issue for months without recognizing progress.[^3]

**The apprentice who seems unteachable is usually a coaching failure, not a learning failure.** If the apprentice can't do a task after three attempts with the same explanation, the explanation is wrong — not the apprentice. Change how you're teaching, not how you're judging.[^3]

---

## Diagram

*(No diagram required for this topic — process/communication content)*

---

## Key terms

- **Coaching:** a structured method of developing skills through demonstration, observation, and feedback
- **Expectations:** the clear statement of the standard and behavior before a task begins
- **Demonstration:** showing the correct technique at real and reduced speed before the apprentice attempts it
- **Observation:** watching the apprentice perform without interruption (except for safety)
- **Feedback:** structured communication that reinforces correct behavior and specifies one improvement
- **Self-assessment:** the apprentice's ability to evaluate their own work — the goal of progressive coaching
- **Journeyperson obligation:** the legal and professional responsibility of a certified tradesperson to supervise and develop apprentices under Alberta AIT and the OHS Act

---

## Common exam trap

- **The Red Seal RSOS does include mentoring (A-6.02)** even though it is weighted 0 questions in the exam blueprint. Knowledge of mentoring principles may appear as context in questions about supervisory responsibility or A-3 safety tasks.
- **Feedback should be specific, not general.** "Good job" is not feedback. "Your electrode angle was consistent for the first pass" is feedback.
- **Interrupting mid-task should be reserved for safety** — not for technique corrections that can wait until the pass is complete.
- **As a journeyperson, you are not just morally responsible — you are legally responsible** for the safety of the apprentice working under your supervision. The OHS Act places this obligation on employers and supervisors, which includes journeypersons in supervisory roles.

---

## Practice question preview

**Q:** A journeyperson welder is coaching an apprentice on 3G root passes. The apprentice runs a pass with inconsistent arc length but finishes without a safety incident. What is the best next step for the journeyperson?

A) Take over and run the next pass correctly without comment  
B) Tell the apprentice they did it wrong and explain all five things to improve  
C) Ask the apprentice how they think the pass went, then address the one most important issue — arc length — with a demonstration  
D) Have the apprentice observe the journeyperson run ten more passes before attempting again

**Correct: C**

**Explanation:** Effective coaching follows the Ask → Reinforce → One Improvement → Demonstrate → Repeat sequence. Asking first develops self-assessment. Limiting feedback to the one most critical issue prevents overwhelm. A demonstration of the correct behavior is more effective than verbal description alone. Option A deprives the apprentice of a learning opportunity. Option B overwhelms with too many correction points. Option D is excessive observation time — the apprentice learns by doing, not by watching repetitively without feedback.

**Red Seal mapping:** A-6.02 (Uses mentoring techniques)

---

[^1]: [Red Seal Occupational Standard — Welder (2024)](https://www.red-seal.ca/eng/trades/welder.shtml); A-6.02 performance criteria — demonstrate tasks, provide feedback, set expectations
[^2]: [Alberta Apprenticeship and Industry Training — Apprenticeship Framework](https://www.alberta.ca/apprenticeship-and-industry-training); journeyperson obligations, supervision ratios, record of training requirements
[^3]: [CWB Group — Welding Supervisor and Trainer Resources](https://www.cwbgroup.org/education); four-step coaching model, feedback principles, on-the-job training best practices
[^4]: [CSA W117.2 — Safety in Welding, Cutting, and Allied Processes](https://www.csagroup.org/store/product/CSA%20W117%3A2/); Clause 4 (employer/supervisor responsibilities), immediate stop authority, PPE compliance obligations
